items.headline: WSJ: White House to name Nvidia, OpenAI, Anthropic and 20+ others AI 'national champions'
items.caption: A new program would back more than two dozen US AI firms as they compete for business abroad. What the label actually gives them is still unclear.

Named so far: Nvidia, Amazon, Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic
Goal: help US AI firms win deals overseas
Benefits and timing not yet spelled out

detail: The Trump administration plans to name more than two dozen AI companies as US 'national champions,' the Wall Street Journal reported Monday. Nvidia, Amazon, Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic are among the names reported.
The program is meant to help American AI firms expand overseas and compete with global rivals. Reports say it is not yet clear what support the label would bring, such as export help or financing.
The news lands a day before Nvidia's earnings and two days before Anthropic prices its IPO. The report has not been confirmed by the White House.
money: Government backing can help sales abroad, but it can also bring more political strings. Weigh both before chasing AI stocks on this headline.
If you own an S&P 500 or Nasdaq fund, you already hold several of the named firms. You may not need extra single-stock bets.
Watch for official details. Concrete perks, like export financing, would matter more to earnings than the label itself.
risk: The report is unconfirmed and the program could change or stall.
Close ties to one administration can become a liability if policy shifts.

items.headline: Intel sued by shareholders after a 29% one-day plunge wiped out $140 billion
items.caption: A Michigan pension fund says Intel was slow to reveal how weak PC demand would hit sales. The proposed class action covers buyers from July 23 to Oct. 29.

visual.title: Intel's slide
visual.label: Intel's one-day drop on Oct. 30 after a weak forecast.

detail: Intel shares fell about 28.6% on Oct. 30 after it forecast weaker fourth-quarter sales and profit and warned of a long PC slump. Roughly $140 billion in market value disappeared.

A proposed class action filed Friday in federal court in San Jose says Intel hid how falling PC demand and excess inventory would hurt revenue. It names Intel, CEO Lip-Bu Tan and CFO David Zinsner and seeks unspecified damages.
The suit notes Intel sold $23 billion of stock at $95 a share in mid-August. Tan has blamed supply shortages and a memory chip crunch for weak PC sales. Intel did not immediately comment.
money: If you bought Intel between July 23 and Oct. 29, 2026, you may be part of the class. Watch for a mailed notice and claim form.
Class action payouts are usually small and slow, but filing a claim is free. Keep your trade confirmations.
Lesson: one stock can drop 29% in a day. Keep single stocks a small slice of your money.
risk: Many securities suits are dismissed or settle for a small share of losses.

detail: Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and President Trump are set to sign a joint trade statement in Manila on Tuesday, Nov. 17. Thailand's Cabinet approved it on Nov. 10.

The statement is a step, not the final trade agreement. It doesn't name a tariff rate. Thai goods have paid 12.5% since July 24, and Anutin said he expects about 19%. Thailand agreed last year to remove tariffs on about 99% of US goods.
Trump left for Asia on Monday. After Manila, he heads to Shenzhen and the APEC summit, then three-way nuclear talks with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
money: Thailand makes many electronics parts, car parts and foods sold in the US. A higher tariff could nudge some prices up.
US farm and food exporters could gain if Thailand cuts its tariffs on American goods.
Existing tariffs stay until the full deal is signed, so don't expect price changes right away.

items.headline: Hackers hijack about 64,000 bitcoin mining machines but fail to mine a single block
items.caption: Attackers pointed about 13 EH/s of hashpower at the OCEAN pool with their own payout address. They earned nothing, but miners lost revenue.

visual.title: The mining hijack
visual.label: Mining machines reportedly taken over Nov. 14-15.

detail: Starting around 8 p.m. Central time on Nov. 14, attackers took over roughly 64,000 bitcoin mining machines. They redirected about 13 EH/s of hashpower to the OCEAN pool and set the payout to an address they controlled.
Hosting firm CoreX raised the alarm. OCEAN's hashrate briefly neared 50 EH/s. CoreX later said the hijacked power fell to about 100 PH/s and the attack appeared to end Nov. 15.
The attackers mined no blocks. But affected miners lost the revenue they would have earned. One operator blamed Luxor's Commander management software, which has not been confirmed.
money: If you own mining stocks, ask how they secure their fleet software. Lost hashing time is lost revenue.
Self-hosting a miner? Change default passwords and lock down remote management tools.
Security incidents keep piling up in crypto. Keep crypto a small part of your money.
risk: The full scope and cause are not yet verified.
Similar attacks could hit other mining software.

detail: California's Department of Financial Protection and Innovation (DFPI) ordered financial institutions to report how they are disbursing insurance payouts from the LA wildfires. It is investigating reports of delayed or denied payments.
When a home has a mortgage, insurance checks often go through the lender, which can release money in stages. Homeowners have complained this slows rebuilding.
The DFPI also notes a law, AB 1847, on extended wildfire-related mortgage forbearance, from 12 to up to 24 months. And it will host free holiday fraud webinars on Nov. 30 and Dec. 2.
money: Waiting on a fire payout held by your lender? Ask in writing for its release schedule and what documents it needs.
If your lender stalls, you can file a complaint with the DFPI.

detail: United said it will restrict personal AI agents that try to book or manage trips for customers. The rule covers its own app and site, plus online travel agencies and aggregators.

The airline says handing logins to an AI tool can expose personal data. Agents could also make purchases, change accounts or redeem MileagePlus miles without the customer meaning to. It also points to rules like the bag safety confirmation at check-in.
Rivals are moving the other way. Southwest launched a ChatGPT flight search plug-in, and OpenAI bought AI travel agent Odessia. United CEO Scott Kirby said he doesn't want another middleman.
money: Don't give your airline password to an AI tool. A hijacked account can drain miles worth hundreds of dollars.
AI agents can still help compare fares. Book the final ticket yourself on the airline's site.
Turn on alerts for mileage redemptions so you catch any action you didn't make.
risk: Agents that break the rules could get your account flagged.
Other airlines may follow with their own limits.

items.headline: DeepMind's AI proves key parts of Signal's encryption secure in four weeks
items.caption: A new DeepMind tool, AlphaProof Code, machine-checked core Signal security guarantees. It found no new holes but did catch old bugs planted back in.

visual.title: AlphaProof Code vs. Signal
items: Took about 4 weeks, building on past work
Proofs checked in the Lean language
Found no new flaws in the parts it checked
Caught 2 old bugs the team planted back in
Did not cover the whole Signal app

detail: Google DeepMind said its new AlphaProof Code system formally verified several core security guarantees of the Signal messaging protocol. The proof of concept took about four weeks, with a head start from earlier verification work.

To test it, the team put two previously fixed bugs back into a copy of Signal's code. The tool produced machine-checked proofs that the buggy versions were insecure. It found no new flaws in the parts it reviewed.
Limits are real. It didn't cover the full mobile app, Google didn't share the cost, and researchers say scaling it up has a long way to go.
money: AI that checks code could cut the cost of security bugs, a big expense for software companies.
Cybersecurity and dev-tool firms may see new competition or new products from this. Watch their guidance.
For you: keep messaging apps updated. Fixes only help once installed.
risk: Results cover only part of the code.
Costs and scale are unknown.

items.headline: Oregon property taxes are due today: pay in full to get a 3% discount
items.caption: Because Nov. 15 fell on a Sunday, Oregon's first property tax payment is due Monday. Paying the full year now earns a 3% discount.

items.t: Last day to appeal your value

Pay the whole bill by the deadline and you get a 3% discount. Pay two-thirds and you get 2%. Pay at least one-third to stay current, with the rest due Feb. 15 and May 17. Mailed payments must be postmarked by the due date.

money: On a $4,000 bill, paying in full saves $120. That beats most savings accounts for the same cash.
Use eCheck, not a credit card. A 2.55% card fee eats most of the 3% discount.
If your value looks too high, file an appeal by Dec. 31. A lower value cuts future bills too.
risk: Bank bill-pay counts when funds arrive, so a same-day send may be late.
Don't drain your emergency fund to grab the discount.

items.headline: Democrats eye the Social Security tax cap: high earners could pay $6,700 more

detail: Social Security tax is 6.2% for workers, matched by employers, but only on wages up to a cap. The cap is $184,500 this year and $192,300 in 2027. Sen. Bernie Sanders says lifting it and raising benefits $2,400 a year are top goals now that Democrats will control Congress.

A Tax Policy Center economist estimated a $300,000 cap would cost a worker at that pay about $6,700 more a year. People earning $150,000 would see no change. Removing the cap would close about 58% of the program's long-term gap.
money: If you earn above the cap, watch this debate when planning bonuses, raises or job offers.
Self-employed high earners pay both halves, so a change would hit them twice as hard; plan estimated taxes accordingly.
Retirement income like IRA withdrawals isn't hit by payroll tax, so this mainly affects wages.
risk: Nothing has passed, and the president could veto changes.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said it will take time to get back to full capacity, but expects normal operations by Thanksgiving. He is pushing for $50 billion in air traffic control upgrades.

risk: Airlines still have to reposition planes and crews, so delays can linger for days.
Aging FAA systems mean repeat outages are possible.

Legal aid groups can help free of charge if your paperwork is complicated.
